title: What training and checking does CASA Part 121 require of airlines operating larger aeroplanes?
description: CASA Part 119 and Part 121 training and checking rules for larger aeroplane operators: the system, head of training and checking, checks and records.
shortAnswer: The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) requires every Australian air transport operator to have a training and checking system and a head of training and checking under Part 119 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998. For multi-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 passenger seats or a maximum take-off weight above 8,618 kg, Part 121 sets the crew requirements: initial and conversion training, proficiency checks, annual line, refresher and emergency equipment checks, and 3 yearly emergency equipment checks.
keyTakeaways: Part 121 applies to multi-engine aeroplanes in Australian air transport operations with a maximum operational passenger seat configuration above 9 or a maximum take-off weight above 8,618 kg (regulation 121.005).

Regulation 119.170 requires a training and checking system with an auditable record system, procedures for completing training and supervision, competence assessment methods, and controls over contracted trainers.

Each flight crew member needs a valid Part 121 proficiency check, refresher check, annual emergency and safety equipment check and 3 yearly emergency and safety equipment check, plus recurrent flight training within the previous 12 months (regulation 121.570).
A proficiency check is valid for up to 8 months from completion, or up to 12 months from the earlier check where checks are done more often (regulation 121.575).
Training and checking records for flight and cabin crew must be made within 21 days of the activity (regulation 119.225).
regulator: Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), under Parts 119 and 121 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 and the Part 121 Manual of Standards
appliesTo: Australian air transport operators of multi-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 passenger seats or a maximum take-off weight above 8,618 kg
Heads of training and checking and the check pilots and examiners they oversee
Flight crew: pilots in command, co-pilots, cruise relief co-pilots and flight engineers
Cabin crew and senior cabin crew members

blocks.text: Part 121, titled "Australian air transport operations: larger aeroplanes" in the [Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F1998B00220/latest/text), applies to multi-engine aeroplanes used in Australian air transport operations where the aeroplane has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9, a maximum take-off weight of more than 8,618 kg, or both (regulation 121.005).

Training and checking obligations sit in two places. Part 119, which certifies Australian air transport operators, requires the training and checking system and the head of training and checking. Part 121 sets the specific crew training, checking and recent experience requirements in Subpart 121.N (flight crew) and Subpart 121.P (cabin crew), with detail prescribed in the Part 121 Manual of Standards.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects Compilation No. 103 of CASR (compilation date September 29, 2026) as at November 2026. The content of recurrent flight training and cabin crew training is prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards, which was not reviewed for this page.

sections.heading: What must the training and checking system contain?

blocks.text: Regulation 119.170 requires every Australian air transport operator to have a training and checking system. For flight crew and cabin crew it must include:

items: A description of how training and checking, including recurrent training and line checking, is conducted by or for the operator.
An auditable system for maintaining records of the results of training and checking.
Procedures ensuring each crew member completes training and checking under the system and is supervised effectively during it.
A description of how the operator assesses each crew member's competence to perform their assigned duties.
For contracted training or checking, details of the contractor, the training covered and how the operator ensures the contractor complies with its system.

blocks.text: For operators of larger aeroplanes, regulation 119.170(4) and (5) extend the system to other operational safety-critical personnel, with the same need for an auditable record system. Regulation 121.485 makes it a strict liability offense, with a penalty of 50 penalty units, to assign a person to flight crew duty without assessing them as competent under the training and checking system. That is a [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) obligation, not just a course completion one.

sections.heading: What qualifications must the head of training and checking hold?

blocks.text: Regulation 119.036 requires every Australian air transport operator to have a position that heads the training and checking part of the organization. Under regulation 119.145, the person must:

items: Hold an air transport pilot licence, or a commercial pilot licence if the operator conducts only single-pilot operations.
Hold a type or class rating for an aircraft used for a significant proportion of the operator's operations.
Have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations, and of training and checking for air operations.
Have sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to run operations safely and in line with the exposition and civil aviation legislation.

sections.heading: Which recurrent checks must flight crew hold?

blocks.text: Under regulation 121.570, a flight crew member meets the recurrent requirements only if they hold four valid checks for the operator and aeroplane and have completed recurrent flight training within the previous 12 months. Crew on unsupervised line flying also need a valid line check.

blocks.text: For the line, refresher and emergency equipment checks, completing a new check less than 3 months before expiry carries the validity forward from the old expiry date. Under regulation 121.580, a pilot proficiency check must be conducted by a person employed by the operator, or by a [Part 142 operator](/regulations/casa-part-141-and-142-flight-training-organisations) under contract, who holds a flight examiner rating for the aeroplane kind (or a CASA approval) and has completed training in human factors principles and non-technical skills.

sections.heading: What initial, command and cabin crew training is required?

blocks.text: Before flying, each flight crew member must meet the operator's initial and conversion training requirements (regulations 121.555 and 121.560). Initial training must meet the Part 121 Manual of Standards and end with an initial training check in accordance with the exposition. Command training under regulation 121.565 includes flying training in the aeroplane or an approved simulator, a Part 121 proficiency check for a pilot in command, and training in pilot in command responsibilities.

Cabin crew requirements in regulation 121.640 mirror the flight crew structure: recent experience, initial, conversion and differences training, a valid annual training check, a valid 3 yearly training check, and, for unsupervised line flying, a valid line check. Under regulation 121.705, each cabin crew member must have flown on the aeroplane type, or completed the operator's refresher training for it, within 6 months before the flight.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each check to the procedures, equipment and competencies it covers, so a change to an aircraft procedure shows which training, check forms and crew records are affected. That supports the auditable record and competence assessment elements of the training and checking system.

faqs.q: Can a Part 142 organization conduct an airline's proficiency checks?
faqs.a: Yes. Regulation 121.580 allows a pilot proficiency check to be conducted by an individual employed by a Part 142 operator with which the airline has a contract to conduct the check. The individual must hold a flight examiner rating for the aeroplane kind or a CASA approval, and have completed human factors and non-technical skills training. The airline's system must describe and control the contract.

faqs.q: How long is a Part 121 proficiency check valid?
faqs.a: Under regulation 121.575, it is valid until the earliest of the next proficiency check, the end of 8 months from completion, or, if the person completed earlier proficiency checks within the preceding 12 months, the end of 12 months from the most recent of those.

faqs.q: Does Part 121 apply to small turboprop operators?
faqs.a: It depends on the aeroplane. Part 121 applies to multi-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 passenger seats or a maximum take-off weight above 8,618 kg. Aeroplanes with no more than 9 seats and no more than 8,618 kg fall under Part 135 (regulation 135.005), and single-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 seats but no more than 8,618 kg fall under Subpart 121.Z.

faqs.q: What records must be made after a training event?
faqs.a: Regulation 119.225 requires the operator to record, within 21 days, when the training, check or assessment took place and whether it was successfully completed. It covers flight crew training and checks under Subpart 121.N, cabin crew training under Subpart 121.P, human factors and non-technical skills training, and safety management system training.
